basic_information.name: AI Energy & Power Infrastructure Economics
basic_information.description: Comprehensive analysis of the energy and power infrastructure economics underpinning AI data centers. Covers electricity consumption forecasts (415 TWh in 2024 rising to 945 TWh by 2030 per IEA), nuclear power deals (Microsoft-Constellation TMI restart, Oracle SMRs, Meta 6.6 GW nuclear commitment), natural gas expansion, cooling technology shifts, capital investment requirements ($5.2-7.9 trillion by 2030 per McKinsey), and regulatory frameworks (EU Energy Efficiency Directive, Germany EnEfG). Energy is emerging as the binding constraint on AI scaling, turning power infrastructure into a strategic moat for hyperscalers.

business_model_structure.revenue_model: Multiple revenue models converge in this space: (1) Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) — long-term contracts (10-20 years) between generators and hyperscalers (e.g., Microsoft-Constellation 20-year, 835 MW nuclear PPA; Meta-Constellation 1.1 GW Clinton reactor PPA); (2) Usage-based utility pricing — traditional $/MWh from grid operators; (3) Infrastructure-as-a-Service — colocation providers bundling power with rack space; (4) Equipment sales — fuel cell and cooling system vendors (Bloom Energy $502M order from Quanta subsidiary); (5) Behind-the-meter generation — hyperscalers building their own natural gas plants or contracting dedicated nuclear reactors.
business_model_structure.pricing_strategy: Power pricing varies dramatically by source and contract type. Grid wholesale electricity: $35-77/MWh depending on source (onshore wind ~$25/MWh, solar ~$26/MWh, combined-cycle gas ~$37/MWh, nuclear ~$77/MWh at $100/tonne carbon price). PPA pricing for solar in ERCOT (Texas): $35-45/MWh, national average $52-58/MWh. PJM capacity market cleared at $329.17/MW-day for 2026-2027 (up 833% from prior year). Wholesale electricity costs up 267% in five years near data center clusters. Data center operators increasingly pay premium prices for 24/7 carbon-free baseload power, with nuclear PPAs commanding significant premiums over intermittent renewables.
business_model_structure.cost_structure: AI data center CapEx structure: GPUs/chips represent over 50% of total ($250-300B of $400-450B global AI CapEx in 2026), followed by construction, land, power infrastructure, and permitting. A 100 MW hyperscale AI data center costs $3.4-5.5B ($34-55M/MW). OpEx breakdown: maintenance ~40%, electricity 15-25%, labor, water, and G&A. Power generation infrastructure: Constellation TMI restart costs $1.6B for 835 MW. Grid upgrade costs estimated at $720B globally by 2030. Cooling infrastructure transitioning from air to liquid, with liquid cooling market growing from $5.1B (2025) to $16.16B (2030).
business_model_structure.value_proposition: Reliable, scalable, 24/7 power supply that enables AI workloads to run continuously without grid constraints. For hyperscalers, securing dedicated power capacity is becoming a competitive advantage — those who lock in long-term clean power agreements gain both operational certainty and ESG compliance. Nuclear offers uniquely high capacity factors (>90%) versus solar (~25%) or wind (~35%), making it ideal for always-on AI training and inference loads. Behind-the-meter generation eliminates grid interconnection bottlenecks that can delay data center deployment by 3-5 years.
business_model_structure.target_customer: Hyperscale cloud providers (Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Meta, Oracle), AI labs (OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI), colocation operators (Equinix, Digital Realty, CoreWeave), government/defense AI programs
business_model_structure.distribution_channel: Direct long-term PPAs, utility tariff rates, behind-the-meter generation, wholesale energy markets (PJM, ERCOT, CAISO), equipment OEM sales, project finance and build-transfer arrangements
business_model_structure.monetization_timeline: Power infrastructure projects have long monetization horizons. Nuclear restarts: 2-5 years to revenue (TMI restart expected 2027, previously 2028). SMR new builds: 8-12 years (Oracle SMR likely mid-2030s; Google-Kairos first unit 2030). Natural gas plants: 2-3 years from permitting to operations. Solar/wind PPAs: 1-2 years. Grid upgrades: ongoing multi-year capital programs. Once operational, assets generate predictable revenue for 20-40+ years (Constellation targeting TMI operations to at least 2054).

financial_metrics.revenue_range: Constellation Energy: projected Free Cash Flow ~$3.6B in 2026, growing to ~$7.9B by 2035. Stock rallied 57.9% in 2025. After Calpine acquisition (closed Jan 2026), fleet includes 21 nuclear reactors and 50+ gas plants. Bloom Energy: $502M fuel cell order from Quanta/QMN plus $5B Brookfield partnership. Global utility CapEx: $212B in 2025 (22% YoY increase), >$1T cumulative over 2025-2029 for 47 largest US investor-owned utilities. Hyperscaler power-related spending embedded in $371B total AI data center CapEx in 2025, rising to ~$400B in 2026.
financial_metrics.gross_margin: Nuclear power plants: gross margins typically 50-70% once operational due to near-zero fuel costs and high capacity factors. Natural gas generation: 30-50% margins depending on gas prices and heat rate. Solar/wind under PPA: margins for developers typically 15-30%. Data center operators pay 15-25% of OpEx on electricity; improving PUE from 1.4 to 1.15 saves ~18% on total power costs. Liquid cooling can reduce cooling energy by 15-50% depending on technology (cold plate: 15%, two-phase immersion: 20%).
financial_metrics.burn_rate: Not directly applicable as a burn rate metric, but project-level capital intensity is extreme: TMI restart $1.6B (with $1B DOE loan), Stargate Phase 1 $100B immediate deployment, full $500B over 4 years. Individual hyperscaler AI CapEx: Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Meta each spending $50-80B annually on data centers (2025-2026).
financial_metrics.cac_ltv_ratio: Not applicable in traditional SaaS sense. For power infrastructure, equivalent metric is capital cost per MW vs. lifetime revenue per MW. Nuclear: ~$1.9M/MW restart cost (TMI) generating revenue over 27+ remaining years. New-build SMR: estimated $5-10M/MW with 40-60 year operational life. Solar PPA: developer capex ~$0.8-1.2M/MW with 15-25 year contract terms.
financial_metrics.funding_total: Constellation Energy: $1B DOE loan for TMI restart (of $1.6B total project cost). Oklo: public via SPAC, market cap $8.88B. TerraPower: raised $750M+ (including $250M from SK Group in 2022). Kairos Power: $303M from DOE Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program. Bloom Energy: $5B Brookfield investment commitment. Stargate LLC: $500B planned investment (OpenAI, SoftBank, Oracle, MGX). Project-level: PJM grid consumers paying $16.6B for power supply security 2025-2027.
financial_metrics.valuation: Constellation Energy: ~$85B market cap (as of early 2026), with analysts setting 12-month target of ~$406. Oklo: $8.88B market cap (248% gain in 6 months). NuScale: received Standard Design Approval May 2025. Bloom Energy: benefiting from $5B Brookfield partnership and major data center orders. Nuclear energy stocks broadly surged in 2025 on AI data center demand narrative. The entire AI power infrastructure investment opportunity is estimated at $5.2-7.9 trillion globally through 2030 (McKinsey).
financial_metrics.arr_growth_rate: Constellation Energy: expected revenue growth 11% and earnings growth 22.5% for 2026. Utility sector CapEx growing 22% YoY in 2025. Data center liquid cooling market CAGR 25.7% (2025-2026). Global data center electricity demand growing at 15-20% annually. Nuclear power capacity under contract to tech companies growing exponentially: Meta alone signed 6.6 GW in January 2026.
financial_metrics.path_to_profitability: Most power generation assets are already profitable or project profitability upon commissioning. Constellation Energy is highly profitable (projected $3.6B FCF in 2026). Nuclear restarts (TMI) expected profitable from day one of operations given locked-in PPA pricing. SMR startups (Oklo, Kairos, TerraPower) are pre-revenue and likely 8-12 years from first commercial power delivery. Natural gas plants profitable within 1-2 years of operation. The key risk is construction cost overruns and delays — NuScale's UAMPS project was cancelled in 2023 due to cost escalation from $5.3B to $9.3B.

market_positioning.competitive_landscape: The AI power infrastructure landscape has distinct tiers: (1) Incumbent nuclear operators — Constellation Energy (dominant, 21 reactors post-Calpine), Vistra, NextEra Energy; (2) SMR/advanced nuclear startups — Oklo, TerraPower, Kairos Power, NuScale, X-Energy; (3) Natural gas turbine manufacturers — GE Vernova (dominant position with gas turbines), Siemens Energy; (4) Fuel cell/distributed generation — Bloom Energy; (5) Grid operators and utilities — PJM, ERCOT, Dominion Energy; (6) Cooling technology — Vertiv, CoolIT Systems, GRC, Schneider Electric. Competition is intensifying as hyperscalers compete for limited grid capacity and available generation assets.
market_positioning.market_size_tam: Total addressable market for AI data center power infrastructure is massive and multi-layered: (1) Global AI data center CapEx: $400-450B in 2026; (2) Grid upgrades: $720B needed by 2030; (3) Total data center power infrastructure investment: $5.2-7.9 trillion through 2030 (McKinsey); (4) Data center liquid cooling: $5.1B in 2025 growing to $16.16B by 2030; (5) US utility CapEx: >$1T cumulative 2025-2029; (6) Power demand: 156 GW of AI data center capacity needed by 2030 (125 incremental GW from 2025). Source: McKinsey (2025), IEA (2025), GlobeNewsWire (2026).
market_positioning.differentiation: Power source choice is becoming a key differentiator: Nuclear offers 24/7 carbon-free baseload with >90% capacity factors but long lead times. Natural gas provides fast deployment (2-3 years) but carbon emissions. Solar/wind are cheapest per MWh but intermittent. Behind-the-meter generation eliminates 3-5 year grid interconnection delays. Companies differentiating on: (1) Speed of power availability; (2) Carbon-free commitments for ESG; (3) Long-term price certainty via PPAs; (4) Scale of secured capacity (Meta: 6.6 GW nuclear, Stargate: up to 10 GW); (5) Cooling efficiency innovation (liquid cooling reduces PUE from 1.4 to <1.2).
market_positioning.moat_type: Multiple moat types converge: (1) Regulatory — nuclear licensing takes 5-10 years, creating massive barriers to entry; NRC licensing is a key bottleneck; (2) Scale — only hyperscalers can sign multi-billion dollar, 20-year PPAs; (3) Switching costs — once a data center is built around specific power infrastructure, switching is extremely expensive; (4) Network effects — grid interconnection rights become more scarce as capacity fills; (5) Technology — advanced reactor designs (Kairos molten salt, TerraPower Natrium, NuScale VOYGR) require decades of R&D; (6) First-mover — companies locking in nuclear PPAs now secure finite clean baseload capacity.
market_positioning.market_share: Constellation Energy is the dominant US nuclear operator with 21 reactors post-Calpine acquisition. In data center power: US data centers consumed ~19 GW in 2023, projected to reach 35 GW by 2030 (FERC). PJM region (Illinois to North Carolina) is the largest data center power market. Virginia alone houses ~70% of global internet traffic infrastructure. Nuclear provides ~18% of US electricity but is becoming disproportionately important for data centers due to 24/7 availability.

ai_specific_economics.compute_cost_ratio: In AI data centers, electricity represents 15-25% of operating expenses. However, the compute (GPU) hardware dominates CapEx at over 50% of total investment ($250-300B of $400-450B global AI CapEx in 2026). Servers account for ~60% of electricity demand within data centers. Cooling consumes 38-40% of total data center power. The AI-specific power premium is substantial: AI-optimized racks draw 40-100+ kW versus 7-15 kW for traditional IT racks, requiring 4-10x more power per rack.
ai_specific_economics.data_advantage: Power availability data and grid capacity intelligence are becoming proprietary advantages. Companies with deep relationships with utilities and grid operators gain early access to available capacity. Historical power consumption patterns help optimize PPA negotiation and capacity planning. Weather data for renewable forecasting. Cooling efficiency data from liquid cooling deployments informs next-generation facility design. Grid stress data helps identify optimal data center locations before competitors.
ai_specific_economics.model_dependency: Power infrastructure is model-agnostic but GPU-generation dependent. NVIDIA H100: 700W TDP per GPU. NVIDIA B200: 1,000-1,200W TDP (43-71% increase over H100). Each new GPU generation increases power per chip but improves performance/watt. GB200 NVL72 racks can draw 120+ kW per rack. The trend toward larger models and longer training runs (months at a time) means power must be 100% reliable — any interruption wastes millions in lost training progress. Inference workloads (80-90% of AI energy consumption globally) are more distributed but growing rapidly.
ai_specific_economics.api_cost_structure: Electricity cost flows through to AI API pricing but represents a minority of total cost. Estimated breakdown of AI inference cost: GPU amortization 50-60%, electricity 10-20%, cooling 5-10%, networking 5-10%, software/overhead 10-15%. At $50-60/MWh average electricity cost and 700W per H100 GPU, a single GPU costs ~$0.035-0.042/hour in electricity alone. Training a frontier model (GPT-4 class) costs an estimated $50-100M+ in total compute, of which electricity is roughly $5-15M. These costs are passed through to API consumers in token-based pricing.
ai_specific_economics.inference_cost_trend: Inference costs per token have been declining 10x every 18-24 months due to hardware efficiency gains, model optimization, and economies of scale. However, total inference energy consumption is growing because demand is growing faster than efficiency gains. Goldman Sachs estimates AI will drive a 165% increase in data center power demand by 2030. Efficiency improvements: PUE trending from 1.4 to 1.15 (best-in-class), liquid cooling saving 15-50% on cooling energy, and new GPU architectures improving performance/watt by 2-4x per generation.
ai_specific_economics.training_cost_economics: Training frontier models requires enormous sustained power: a 100,000 GPU H100 cluster draws ~70 MW continuously for months. At $50/MWh, that is ~$2.5M/month in electricity alone. The trend toward larger clusters (Stargate targeting 1 GW+ campuses) means training costs are dominated by GPU CapEx but power availability is the binding constraint. Companies unable to secure sufficient power simply cannot train competitive frontier models, making power infrastructure a prerequisite for participation in the AI race. Power costs are expected to decline per unit of useful compute as efficiency improves, but total power spending will increase as workloads scale.
ai_specific_economics.energy_cost_factor: Energy is transitioning from a secondary cost factor to a primary strategic constraint. While electricity is only 15-25% of data center OpEx, it is the binding constraint on where and how fast new capacity can be built. Grid interconnection delays (3-5 years) are now longer than data center construction times (18-24 months). This mismatch makes power infrastructure the critical bottleneck in AI scaling. Companies that secure power first can build AI capacity first — power access is becoming as important as GPU access in the AI supply chain.

scaling_and_growth.growth_strategy: Growth in AI power infrastructure is driven by: (1) Hyperscaler CapEx commitments ($400B+ in 2026); (2) Government support (DOE $1B loan for TMI, Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program); (3) Long-term PPAs providing revenue certainty for generation investment; (4) Behind-the-meter and on-site generation to bypass grid bottlenecks; (5) Project Stargate as a catalytic $500B commitment; (6) Vertical integration — hyperscalers building their own power plants (natural gas facilities tripled in US in 2025); (7) International expansion to regions with abundant cheap power (Nordics, Middle East, Canada).
scaling_and_growth.network_effects: Limited direct network effects but strong indirect effects: (1) Grid interconnection capacity becomes scarcer as more data centers connect, increasing the value of secured capacity; (2) Power infrastructure development attracts adjacent investment (cooling, networking, talent); (3) Nuclear licensing precedents (NuScale Standard Design Approval) reduce regulatory costs for subsequent plants; (4) Scale of PPAs — the larger a buyer's commitment, the more favorable pricing they can negotiate; (5) Ecosystem development — SMR supply chains become viable only with sufficient order volume from tech companies.
scaling_and_growth.flywheel_description: The AI power infrastructure flywheel operates as follows: Hyperscaler AI demand drives massive power requirements -> Power scarcity creates premium pricing and long-term PPA commitments -> Premium pricing justifies investment in new generation (nuclear restarts, SMR development, gas plants) -> New generation capacity enables more AI compute deployment -> More AI compute deployment drives more demand for power -> Cycle accelerates. A secondary flywheel: efficiency improvements (liquid cooling, better PUE) free up power capacity within existing facilities, enabling more GPU density, which drives more cooling innovation.
scaling_and_growth.scalability_model: Improving unit economics at scale, with important caveats. Nuclear: excellent once built (near-zero marginal fuel cost, 40-60 year lifespan, >90% capacity factor), but construction is the bottleneck (TMI restart: $1.6B, 2+ years). Solar/wind: rapidly declining costs ($25-26/MWh) but intermittency requires storage. Natural gas: fast to deploy but carbon cost risk. Cooling: liquid cooling reduces energy per unit of compute by 15-50%, and the liquid cooling market is scaling rapidly (25.7% CAGR). Overall, power cost per useful unit of AI compute is declining due to efficiency gains, but total power spending is rising dramatically.
scaling_and_growth.geographic_expansion: Power availability is reshaping data center geography. Traditional hubs (Northern Virginia/Loudoun County, Oregon, Netherlands) face grid constraints. Emerging locations driven by power abundance: (1) Texas (ERCOT, cheapest solar, Stargate in Abilene); (2) Nordics (cheap hydro, cold climate reduces cooling); (3) Middle East (Saudi Arabia, UAE — cheap energy, sovereign wealth investment); (4) Canada (hydroelectric); (5) France (nuclear baseload — 70% nuclear grid); (6) Rural US near nuclear plants (Pennsylvania TMI, Ohio Meta). PJM region seeing most acute grid strain with data center capacity auction prices surging 833%.
scaling_and_growth.customer_retention: Extremely high retention due to physical infrastructure lock-in. Once a data center is built at a specific location with specific grid interconnections and power agreements, switching is effectively impossible. PPAs of 10-20 years provide contractual lock-in. Nuclear PPAs (Constellation-Microsoft: 20 years, to 2054) represent some of the longest commitments in the industry. Grid interconnection queue positions are transferable but scarce, creating secondary market value.

key_risks: 1. Demand uncertainty: Utilities are grappling with whether AI data center power demand projections are real. Bloomberg reported Stargate had not started as of August 2025, and some industry observers question whether $500B will materialize. If AI investment slows (as happened briefly with DeepSeek efficiency concerns in January 2025), power infrastructure built on speculative demand could be stranded.

2. Grid infrastructure bottleneck: Grid interconnection delays of 3-5 years are the primary constraint. PJM capacity auction prices surged 833%, and residential electricity consumers face $16-18/month increases due to data center demand. Political backlash from rising consumer energy costs could lead to regulatory restrictions on data center power consumption.

3. Nuclear construction risk: Historical nuclear projects have massive cost overrun track records. NuScale's UAMPS project was cancelled in 2023 after costs escalated from $5.3B to $9.3B. SMR technology is unproven at commercial scale — no SMR is operational in the US. Oracle's SMR data center is likely a decade away.

4. Regulatory and environmental risk: EU Data Centre Energy Efficiency Package (March 2026) may impose minimum performance standards. Germany's EnEfG requires 100% renewable electricity by January 2027. Permitting reform is uncertain. Water usage for cooling faces scrutiny in drought-prone regions. Carbon emission concerns for natural gas plants.

5. Technology disruption: If AI model efficiency improves dramatically (as DeepSeek suggested), power demand forecasts could prove wildly inflated. Conversely, if quantum computing or novel architectures reduce compute needs, massive power infrastructure investments could be stranded. Each generation of GPUs is more power-efficient per computation, potentially bending the demand curve.
risk_and_challenges.regulatory_exposure: High and increasing. EU AI Act (2024) includes energy efficiency and transparency requirements for AI systems. EU Energy Efficiency Directive requires data center reporting on energy consumption, water usage, and renewable energy. European Commission preparing Data Centre Energy Efficiency Package for March 2026 with rating scheme and minimum performance standards. Germany EnEfG mandates 50% renewable energy (current), increasing to 100% by January 2027 for data centers. EU Cloud and AI Development Act aims to triple EU data center capacity while managing energy impacts. In the US, FERC oversight of capacity markets directly affects data center power costs. NRC licensing requirements for nuclear create 5-10 year regulatory timelines.
risk_and_challenges.commoditization_risk: Moderate. Electricity itself is a commodity, but the delivery infrastructure (grid interconnection, behind-the-meter generation, cooling systems) is highly differentiated. Nuclear power's scarcity creates a premium for carbon-free baseload — Constellation's 21 reactors are effectively irreplaceable assets. However, if SMR technology scales successfully, new entrants could increase supply. Solar and wind are rapidly commoditizing. Natural gas generation faces commoditization pressure. The real moat is in securing interconnection rights and long-term PPAs, not in the power generation technology itself.
risk_and_challenges.talent_dependency: Moderate to high. Nuclear engineering talent is scarce (decades of industry contraction in the US). SMR development requires specialized nuclear engineers, regulatory experts, and construction management. Data center electrical infrastructure design requires specialized power systems engineers. Cooling technology innovation requires thermal engineers. However, unlike AI model development, power infrastructure relies more on proven engineering than cutting-edge research, making talent needs more predictable if less abundant.
risk_and_challenges.vendor_lock_in: High for power infrastructure, moderate for cooling. Grid interconnection: once established, extremely costly to relocate (multi-year process, hundreds of millions of dollars). Nuclear PPAs: 20-year contracts with single providers (e.g., Constellation). GPU dependency: NVIDIA dominates AI accelerators, and each GPU generation has different power and cooling requirements, forcing infrastructure upgrades. Cooling vendor lock-in is moderate — liquid cooling standards are emerging but not yet universal. Cloud provider dependency: hyperscalers building proprietary power infrastructure reduce reliance on third-party colocation but create internal lock-in.

entrepreneurial_relevance.startup_applicability: For startups, the AI energy infrastructure landscape presents several opportunities and considerations: (1) DO NOT try to compete in power generation or nuclear — these require billions in capital and decades of regulatory navigation; (2) DO consider adjacent opportunities: cooling technology innovation (liquid cooling market growing 25.7% CAGR to $16.16B by 2030), power monitoring and optimization software, energy efficiency consulting for data centers, PPA brokerage and advisory services, grid interconnection queue management tools; (3) Edge AI and energy-efficient inference hardware offer startup-scale opportunities to reduce dependence on massive centralized infrastructure; (4) European startups should leverage EU regulations (Energy Efficiency Directive reporting requirements) as a business opportunity; (5) Power cost awareness is critical for any AI startup — understand that electricity is 15-25% of OpEx and model it into unit economics from day one.
entrepreneurial_relevance.build_vs_buy_guidance: For AI startups: ALWAYS buy power infrastructure — never build. Use cloud providers (AWS, Azure, GCP) who have already secured massive power capacity through PPAs and behind-the-meter generation. The capital requirements ($34-55M per MW for AI data centers) and timelines (2-5 years for power infrastructure) are incompatible with startup economics. For AI-adjacent startups in the energy space: consider building specialized software/services that help data center operators optimize power usage, cooling efficiency, or regulatory compliance. For larger scale-ups approaching hyperscaler compute needs: negotiate custom cloud contracts that include power cost transparency, and evaluate colocation in regions with abundant cheap power (Texas, Nordics, Canada).
key_lessons: 1. Power is the new GPU bottleneck: Securing AI compute is no longer just about GPU availability — it is equally about power availability. Grid interconnection delays (3-5 years) now exceed data center construction times (18-24 months). Startups should factor regional power availability into their cloud provider and colocation decisions.

2. Energy costs compound at scale: At startup scale, electricity is negligible. At scale, it becomes 15-25% of OpEx. Model energy costs into unit economics early, especially if running inference workloads (80-90% of global AI energy consumption). A single H100 GPU costs ~$0.035-0.042/hour in electricity alone.

3. The $5-8 trillion opportunity is real but long-cycle: McKinsey estimates $5.2-7.9 trillion in AI power infrastructure investment by 2030. This creates enormous opportunities for infrastructure-adjacent companies (cooling, monitoring, optimization, consulting) that can serve this market without needing to raise billions in capital themselves.

4. Regulatory compliance is a business opportunity: EU Energy Efficiency Directive reporting requirements, Germany's 100% renewable mandate by 2027, and the upcoming Data Centre Energy Efficiency Package (March 2026) create demand for compliance tools, reporting platforms, and energy efficiency consulting. First movers in regulatory tech for data centers can build strong market positions.

5. Geographic arbitrage matters: Power costs vary 3-5x between regions ($25/MWh in Texas vs. $77+/MWh for nuclear). France's 70% nuclear grid makes it uniquely positioned in Europe for 24/7 carbon-free AI data centers. Startups should consider power economics when choosing where to deploy inference infrastructure.
entrepreneurial_relevance.session_mapping: Session 4 (AI Business Models & Strategy) — power infrastructure economics as a key cost driver and competitive moat in AI business models; also relevant to Session 3 (Build vs. Buy decisions for compute infrastructure) and Session 5 (Ethics/Governance — energy sustainability, EU AI Act energy provisions)

confidence.data_quality: High — sourced from IEA (official energy data), McKinsey, Goldman Sachs Research, S&P Global, BloombergNEF, company IR (Constellation Energy, OpenAI, Meta announcements), US DOE/FERC, European Commission, IEEE Spectrum, and major financial publications (CNBC, Yahoo Finance). Most data points are from 2025-2026.
confidence.cross_reference: IEA 2025 Energy and AI report confirms 415 TWh (2024) and 945 TWh (2030) projections, consistent with Goldman Sachs 165% demand growth estimate. McKinsey $5.2-7.9T investment estimate aligns with Deloitte's $1T+ utility CapEx projection. Constellation-Microsoft TMI deal details confirmed across Constellation press release, CNBC, IEEE Spectrum, DOE loan announcement. Meta 6.6 GW nuclear deals confirmed by Meta official announcement, CNBC, and NucNet. Stargate $500B confirmed by OpenAI but Bloomberg reported delays in August 2025.
confidence.caveats: AI power demand forecasts are subject to significant uncertainty — projections range from 945 TWh (IEA Base Case) to 1,000+ TWh (Energy Intelligence) by 2026-2030. Demand could be lower if AI efficiency improves dramatically (DeepSeek effect) or if AI investment slows. Nuclear construction timelines are historically unreliable — cost overruns of 2-5x are common. SMR technology is unproven commercially in the US. The $500B Stargate commitment was reported as not started as of August 2025. PPA pricing data may not reflect actual negotiated rates which are commercially confidential. EU regulatory landscape is still evolving with key packages expected in 2026.
